lesson.title: Where does a leaf get its carbon?

lead.text: Sugar is built from carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms. Follow the atoms, not the energy.

reveal.text: You traced the carbon to carbon dioxide. Light provides energy, but it does not supply atoms.

steps.headline: Photosynthesis builds glucose from carbon dioxide and water, using light energy.

lead.text: Written simply: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂.
The sugar is glucose. The numbers in front say how many molecules react, and oxygen leaves as a product.

steps.headline: How many CO₂ molecules must be taken in to make five glucose molecules?

workedSteps.text: One glucose holds six carbon atoms.
Five glucose hold five lots of six.
Each CO₂ brings in one carbon atom, so count them.

steps.headline: How many CO₂ molecules supply the carbon for two glucose molecules?

workedSteps.text: One glucose holds six carbon atoms.
Two glucose hold twice as many.
Each CO₂ brings in one carbon atom.

steps.headline: Light brings energy and no matter. The plant stores it in sugar and later releases it.

lead.text: Photosynthesis captures some light energy and stores it in the bonds of glucose.
Cells can later use that sugar as fuel, in a process called respiration. Plants do both.
A leaf cell has chloroplasts, but that does not make it self-sufficient. At night it still has work to do.

reveal.text: Chloroplasts store energy in sugar. Respiration is what releases it for the cell's work, so a leaf cell needs both.

lead.text: A leaf was given a fixed, low supply of CO₂. Its rate was measured at several light levels. Compare two readings to see what extra light did.

reveal.text: The rate did not change, so light was not what limited it. With so little CO₂, the CO₂ supply set the rate.

lesson.orientation: Trace carbon and energy through the overall photosynthesis reaction.
lesson.reviewLabel: Where does a leaf get its carbon?
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A sapling weighs 2 kg when it is planted in a tub of soil.
Years later it weighs 77 kg. The soil has lost only 60 grams.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say where a leaf's carbon comes from, use the photosynthesis equation to count molecules, and keep matter and energy apart.
intro.whyItMatters: Nearly all the food and fuel we use started as sugar made this way.

recap.keyIdea: Photosynthesis builds sugar from carbon dioxide and water. Light supplies the energy, which the plant stores in the sugar.

blocks.text: You traced a tree's mass to the air and water, then counted CO₂, water and oxygen molecules for several glucose molecules.
You also read a flat curve as a limit set by something other than light.

recap.nextHook: A cell burns sugar to do its work. How does it use that fuel?

questions.prompt: Name the gas that supplies the carbon atoms in a leaf's newly made sugar.
hints: Trace atoms separately from energy.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carbon dioxide supplies the carbon atoms; light supplies energy.

questions.onCorrect: Carbon dioxide. Light brings energy; the atoms for the sugar come from the gas.

misconceptions.feedback: Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis. Look for the gas that contains carbon.
Light is energy. It has no atoms to give.

questions.prompt: One glucose has six carbon atoms. Each CO₂ supplies one. How many CO₂ molecules supply the carbon for two glucose molecules?
hints: Count the carbon atoms in both glucose molecules.
Each glucose has six carbon atoms.
Each CO₂ contributes one carbon atom.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two glucose contain 2 × 6 = 12 carbon atoms, so they need 12 CO₂.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Count the carbon atoms in the sugar, because each came from one CO₂.

misconceptions.feedback: That is enough for one glucose. There are two.
That counts the glucose molecules. Count the carbon atoms.

questions.prompt: In photosynthesis, in what form is light energy stored?
hints: Think of the sugar the plant makes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Photosynthesis captures some incoming light energy as chemical energy in sugar.

questions.onCorrect: Chemical energy, held in the bonds of sugar. Light itself adds no matter.

misconceptions.feedback: Some energy is lost as heat, but the energy that is captured is stored differently.
Carbon is matter. The question asks about the form of the energy.

questions.prompt: With a low supply of CO₂, the photosynthetic rate is 8 at light level 60 and 8 at light level 80. By how much did the rate increase?
hints: Use the two rates given for the lower curve.
Subtract the first rate from the second.
What is the difference between two equal rates?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8 − 8 = 0. The curve is flat between those light levels.

questions.onCorrect: Zero. The curve has plateaued, so something else, here the CO₂ supply, is limiting the rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rate itself, not the change in it.
That is the change in light level, not in the rate.

questions.prompt: A leaf cell has chloroplasts. Name the process, besides photosynthesis, that it uses to transfer energy from sugar.
hints: Photosynthesis does not replace every other cell process.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Leaf cells also respire to support their energy needs.

questions.onCorrect: Respiration. Photosynthesis stores the energy, and respiration releases it for the cell's work.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the process the question rules out. Name the other one.

questions.prompt: Using the simplified overall equation, how many O₂ molecules accompany the formation of three glucose molecules?
hints: Read the number written in front of O₂.
Use that number of oxygen molecules for each glucose.
Multiply by three glucose molecules.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose corresponds to six O₂: 3 × 6 = 18.

questions.onCorrect: 18. Six O₂ come with each glucose, so scale by the number of glucose molecules.

misconceptions.feedback: That is for one glucose. There are three.
That counts the glucose molecules. Multiply by the oxygen made for each one.

questions.prompt: A plant is given CO₂ whose carbon atoms are labelled. Name the kind of molecule the labelled carbon ends up in.
hints: Where does the carbon from CO₂ go?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The carbon from CO₂ is built into sugar such as glucose.

questions.onCorrect: Sugar. The carbon from CO₂ is built into glucose, so the label follows the carbon.

misconceptions.feedback: Oxygen is released as a product, and it comes from water. The label rides on carbon.

questions.prompt: A leaf makes four glucose molecules. How many water molecules does that use, using the simplified equation?
hints: Read the number in front of H₂O.
That number is for one glucose.
Multiply by four glucose molecules.
questions.onCorrect: 24. Six water molecules go in for each glucose, so scale by the number made.

misconceptions.feedback: That is for one glucose. There are four.
That counts the glucose molecules. Multiply by the water used for each.

questions.prompt: Where did nearly all of the tree's new mass come from?
hints: How much mass did the soil lose compared with the tree's gain?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Most of a tree's new mass is built from carbon dioxide in the air and from water.

questions.onCorrect: The air and water. Plants build their bodies from carbon dioxide and water, not from the soil.

misconceptions.feedback: The soil lost almost nothing, so it cannot account for such a large gain.
Light carries energy, but it adds no atoms to the tree.

questions.prompt: In the overall equation, how many CO₂ molecules go in for one glucose molecule?
hints: Read the number written in front of CO₂.
Find CO₂ on the left-hand side of the equation.
It matches the number of carbon atoms in glucose.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The equation starts 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light, so six CO₂ per glucose.

questions.onCorrect: Six. One glucose has six carbon atoms, and each CO₂ brings one.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one glucose. Read the number in front of CO₂.
That is the number of hydrogen atoms in glucose. Read the number in front of CO₂.

questions.prompt: Why does the number of CO₂ molecules equal the number of carbon atoms in the sugar?
hints: Count the carbon atoms inside one CO₂.

acceptedIdeas: Each CO₂ supplies exactly one carbon atom
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each CO₂ contains one carbon atom, and every carbon atom in the sugar came from one.

choices.label: Light supplies the rest of the carbon
Each CO₂ supplies exactly one carbon atom

questions.onCorrect: Each CO₂ carries one carbon atom, so counting carbon atoms counts CO₂ molecules.

misconceptions.feedback: Light is energy and has no atoms.
Water contains hydrogen and oxygen only. The carbon comes from the gas.
